one_liner: Go code generator for a msgpack2 format with integer field keys; marshals ~1.3-4x faster than Go protobuf libraries
what_it_does: A `//go:generate zebrapack` tool, forked from tinylib/msgp, that uses your own Go structs as the schema. You tag fields with `zid:"N"` (the bundled `addzid` tool can add the tags), and it generates MarshalMsg/UnmarshalMsg methods plus optional streaming Encode/Decode methods on those types. The wire format is plain msgpack2, except that structs become maps keyed by small integers instead of field-name strings. The schema can be compiled to msgpack2 or JSON (`-write-schema`) so other languages can map ids back to names. This is not a drop-in replacement for protobuf: there is no .proto IDL, the wire format is not compatible, and schema evolution follows Cap'n Proto-style numbering: add fields with the next id and deprecate them, never delete them.
how_it_is_fast: The generated encoders use no reflection and call msgp.Append* directly. They append into the caller's buffer, which is pre-sized once from an upper-bound Msgsize, so marshaling allocates nothing. Each field key is a single byte (0x0-0x5 in the benchmark struct) instead of a string, so encoding writes fewer bytes and decoding switches on an integer instead of comparing strings. Decoding fills an existing struct in place. With `-fast-strings`, strings are unsafe casts that point into the input buffer (UnsafeZeroCopy), which removes the string allocations. The benchmark also used `-no-structnames-onwire`, which drops the struct-name field that ZebraPack otherwise writes under key -1 on every struct.
when_to_use: Go-to-Go messaging or RPC with small, flat structs where write throughput and zero allocations matter (6-field struct: 120 ns/op marshal, 0 allocs)
You want your existing Go structs to be the schema, with no .proto/.capnp IDL and no protoc or C++ toolchain to maintain
Consumers in dynamic languages already have msgpack2 decoders and can load a separately shipped schema to turn integer keys back into field names
Decode-process-discard pipelines where input buffers are not reused while decoded values are still alive, so `-fast-strings` zero-copy is safe
Maintaining a legacy codebase that already emits ZebraPack data
when_not_to_use: New projects: the author's own repo description points to greenpack as the more recent alternative, and ZebraPack has had no commits since 2018-11-07
Read-heavy workloads: unmarshal (236 ns) only ties FlatBuffers (236) and gogoprotobuf (240), and is slower than Gencode (196) and go-capnproto v1 (210) in the same table
You need protobuf wire compatibility, gRPC tooling, or generated code for languages other than Go; other languages must adapt a msgpack2 library and load the schema themselves
Your protocol needs to tell a zero value from an absent field, or needs required fields: zero-valued fields are left off the wire and decode as zero
Deeply nested structs: the decoder's nil-tracking stack is fixed at 8 levels (MaxNestedStructPointerDepth) and panics if you go past it

integration.form: module (Go code-generator binary run via go generate, plus the runtime package github.com/glycerine/zebrapack/msgp that generated code imports)
integration.dependencies: runtime: github.com/philhofer/fwd; generator: golang.org/x/tools (go/loader, imports). There is no go.mod file (GOPATH-era).
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. The benchmarks ran on Go 1.8beta2, and Travis CI targeted Go 1.x and tip in 2017. Builds on current Go releases were not checked.
integration.platforms: Any Go target in principle. CI covered amd64 and 386. The unsafe string casts sit behind a !appengine build tag, and a safe appengine fallback file exists.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The generated Marshal/Unmarshal methods keep decoder state in locals and touch only the receiver and the buffer passed in, so separate values can be used concurrently. Using one value from several goroutines needs external locking.

gotchas: Every field behaves as if it were omitempty: zero values are never written, so a decoder cannot tell 0/""/false from a missing field. The author confirmed this was deliberate in issue #10.
`-fast-strings` makes decoded strings point into the input []byte. If you reuse or mutate that buffer, strings you already decoded change silently. Copy them if you need them to outlive the buffer.
The published numbers depend on `-fast-strings -no-structnames-onwire`. By default the generator is not zero-copy and writes each struct's name under key -1, which costs time and bytes.

Non-pointer struct-valued fields were encoded incorrectly (inner fields dropped) until the final commit on 2018-11-07 (issue #10). Older vendored copies need that fix; the reporter's workaround was to use pointer fields.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against greenpack (same author, maintained into 2026, 129 ns marshal in the same table), ZebraPack gives a smaller wire and a ~7% write edge. The cost is that data is no longer self-describing (greenpack keeps name+zid+type in field names) and the project is abandoned, so for new Go code pick greenpack. Pick ZebraPack over zero-copy formats such as Karmem or FlatBuffers only when you need msgpack2 wire compatibility and Go structs as the schema.
verified_claims_summary: These numbers come from the author's own fork of alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks, run around 2017 (header says Go 1.8beta2) on a 3.1 GHz Core i7 MacBook Pro 13". ZebraPack marshals a 6-field struct in 120 ns/op with 0 allocs, against 152 ns for gogoprotobuf (~1.27x), 379 ns for FlatBuffers, 498 ns for go-capnproto v1 and 500 ns for golang/protobuf (~4.2x); unmarshal is 236 ns against 701 ns for golang/protobuf (~3x). The comparison favours ZebraPack: it reuses a 512-byte buffer and one target struct and uses zero-copy strings, while the protobuf benchmarks allocate on every call. The table's 'GreenPack' unmarshal row actually calls ZebraPack's ZUnmarshalMsg, so its 224 vs 236 ns gap is run-to-run noise on identical code.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-11-07 and superseded by the author's greenpack. It is MIT-licensed and the runtime msgp package is small enough to vendor, but it has no go.mod, so treat it as legacy code rather than a new dependency.
